College football schedule 2026: What to watch in Week 12, TV channels, streaming, Saturday kickoff times
Multiple College Football Playoff dreams could be dashed in Week 12
By
Austin Nivison
Nov 20, 2026
at
12:53 pm ET
4 min read
Getty Images
We're closing in on the end of the regular season, and there are still conference championship races to be decided and College Football Playoff spots up for grabs. Week 12 will help us sort some of that out with a slate of fascinating matchups all over the country.
No. 14 Ohio State is still holding out hope for a CFP berth, but it has to take freshman quarterback Luke Fahey on the road to play Nebraska, a program starved for a top-25 win and a win over the Buckeyes in general. The Huskers just snapped a four-game losing streak with a blowout win over Rutgers, so perhaps that gives them some confidence as Ohio State rolls into Lincoln.
In the afternoon, a couple of College Football Playoff hopefuls face tricky tests. No. 4 UCLA visits Michigan, and No. 9 Tennessee hosts LSU. The Wolverines' defense is capable of shutting down anyone, and the Tigers have fallen a play or two short of some massive wins this fall.
In the evening, national championship favorites will try to avoid last-minute stumbles. No. 7 Miami faces Virginia Tech, a team capable of testing the Hurricanes' secondary. Additionally, top-ranked Georgia will take its hot streak into a hostile atmosphere against No. 21 South Carolina.
With so many quality games on throughout the day, here's a handy guide to help you prioritize your viewing.
All times Eastern.
The best games
No. 14 Ohio State at Nebraska -- 12 p.m. on Fox,  Fubo (try for free):  Nebraska hasn't beaten Ohio State since 2011, but the Huskers have a great chance to end that streak on Saturday. The Buckeyes simply haven't been the same since Julian Sayin went down with an injury, and the Cornhuskers stopped the bleeding with a 31-0 win over Rutgers last weekend. Quarterback Anthony Colandrea has looked much more comfortable in the Nebraska offense over the last two weeks, and he'll need a clean game to give his team a shot to effectively end the Buckeyes' season.
No. 4 UCLA at Michigan -- 3:30 p.m. on CBS, CBSSports.com, Paramount+ Premium: They may not win any beauty contests, but the Bruins just keep winning. I wouldn't expect things to get any prettier this weekend as UCLA visits Michigan, a team with an abhorrent offense and a great defense. This will be Ty Dieffenbach's biggest challenge since he took over for the injured Nico Iamaleava on Oct. 10. The key for the Bruins will be whether receiver Aidan Mizell can continue his late-season breakout. He's got 326 yards and three touchdowns over the last two games, but the Wolverines' secondary should provide a bigger test.
LSU at No. 9 Tennessee -- 3:30 p.m. on ABC,  Fubo (try for free): LSU has been reduced to the role of spoiler as Tennessee can essentially lock up a College Football Playoff berth with a win. Coming into the season, I thought those roles would be reversed, but these teams have been trending in different directions. Indiana started 7-0 last season and still missed the NCAA Tournament with an 18-14 record. So I understand those with a pump-the-brakes attitude.
But doesn't this start feel different?
It certainly looks different. And in terms of the quality of the wins, it's undeniably different following Friday's 90-76 blowout of Kentucky inside Lucas Oil Stadium that pushed the Hoosiers to 6-0 with three victories over schools ranked inside the top 80 at KenPom. Last season's 7-0 start at Indiana featured zero wins over schools that finished ranked inside the top 80 at KenPom -- and five of those first seven wins were over teams that finished ranked 240th-or-worse.
Again, this season's 6-0 start features three wins over schools ranked inside the top 80 -- specifically Arkansas (No. 38), Kentucky (No. 63) and Syracuse (No. 78). For what it's worth, Arkansas and Kentucky -- John Calipari's current school and his old school -- were both in the preseason AP Top 25 poll, meaning the only schools with multiple wins over teams in the preseason Top 25 are Houston, Memphis and Indiana.
Will this be the season the Hoosiers get back to the Sweet 16 for the first time since Tom Crean guided them there in 2016? As always, we'll see. But there's no denying they're off to a nice start, one that has more substance to it than the start IU put together last season.
Indiana is No. 25 in Saturday morning's updated CBS Sports Top 25 And 1 daily college basketball rankings, where Houston remains No. 1 for the third straight morning. As for Kentucky, I mean, yuck.
As I've noted many times on the Eye On College Basketball Podcast, nobody needed an encouraging start to the season more than third-year UK coach Mark Pope.
So far, it's going terribly.
The Wildcats are 4-2 with no good wins, a 20-point loss to Kansas and a 14-point loss to Indiana. They're down to 63rd at KenPom and 64th at BartTorvik. Even worse, when you remove the preseason data from the rankings at Torvik, Kentucky drops all the way down to 115th.
And did you see the updated projections at KenPom?
It now has the Wildcats entering the SEC Tournament with a 16-16 record, including a 6-12 mark in the SEC. Needless to say, barring something surprising, that would result in a coaching change at UK, a place that has spent big money on rosters each of the past two seasons but is -- to date -- getting a poor return on its investment.

The Indianapolis Colts tried to sit on the fence at the 2026 trade deadline, ship away some (not all) expendable pieces, and land a somewhat respectable, middle-of-the-road record that might save a few jobs in the process. That meant moving on from the likes of DeForest Buckner, Quenton Nelson, and Josh Downs, but holding on to Jonathan Taylor and Daniel Jones. Less than two weeks removed from that semi-fire sale, it's safe to say Indy botched it.
What's the old saying? If you're going to be a bear, be a grizzly. Well, if the Colts felt alright selling some pieces at the deadline, they should've stripped it down to the studs, knowing full well they are entering a rebuild anyway after firing GM Chris Ballard in mid-October.
The losses have only continued to pile up for the Colts, which includes a demoralizing defeat at the hands of the Houston Texans in Week 11. That game, which dropped them to 3-8, proved to be the straw that broke the camel's back for the Daniel Jones era, as the team has since waived the veteran quarterback.

Again, this is a player who teams were reportedly interested in leading up to the deadline. Instead of pursuing those opportunities to shed a sunk-cost under center, ESPN reports that Indy rebuffed trade interest from teams like the Minnesota Vikings and Baltimore Ravens.
As a reminder, the Vikings traded a 2027 third-round pick to acquire Kirk Cousins, while the Ravens shipped a 2027 fourth-round pick and a 2028 seventh-round pick to the Cardinals in exchange for Jacoby Brissett and a 2027 fifth-round pick. It's unclear what the compensation for Jones would've been, but I can tell you this—it's more than what they have now after waiving him: nothing.
In the nine games before the deadline, Jones had the Colts at 2-7 while completing 60.3% of his passes, averaging just 191.3 passing yards per game, and posting a passer rating of 68.9. In total, Jones had tallied seven touchdowns and 13 turnovers.

It was abundantly clear in the lead-up to the deadline that the two-year, $88 million extension the Colts signed Jones this offseason to was a disaster. Miraculously, a lifeboat drifted by them in the form of multiple teams inquiring about taking that burden off their hands, but they decided to stay on the deserted island. Now they're paying the price, with Jones set to account for $35.2 million in dead cap space for 2027 (provided he clears waivers) while the team pays him $49.8 million for 11 games played this season.
On top of Jones, Taylor, arguably the most sought-after prize on the trade market this cycle, should've been firmly on the block. With the Colts now without a clear answer at quarterback, Taylor is the living embodiment of that meme where the Lamborghini is sitting in the driveway of the trailer park.
He was most valuable to Indy as a trade chip at the deadline, and that remains the case this offseason. The only difference is that any team acquiring him is getting a back that's a little older, has a little more mileage, and doesn't help them for this stretch run in 2026. That sets up a possibly diminished return this offseason if/when the Colts deal him compared to what they could've gotten at this deadline.
For a team that won't have its first-round pick in 2027 after trading for Sauce Gardner at last year's deadline, they were in a position to refill the cupboard. Neither Jones nor Taylor likely would've fetched a first-rounder, but they would've given Indy premium ammunition for a later deal that could vault them back up. That level of asset mismanagement around the deadline now has the potential to ripple beyond just this second half of the season.
Jones being waived is just one of the initial steps that the Colts will take as they embark on this rebuild and they tripped out of the gate. Whether it's firing Shane Steichen, trading Taylor, or eventually hiring a new GM (if they can find a taker), the organization needs to have a more definitive and realistic plan for its future so they're not looking back with major second guesses like they currently are following this deadline.

Let's start with the games that have significant College Football Playoff implications. No. 9 Tennessee (8-2) is a 1.5-point home underdog against Lane Kiffin's visiting LSU Tigers. It's a ripe opportunity for Kiffin to spoil his former employer's playoff hopes. Can Tennessee afford a third loss? The CBS Sports forecasting model drops Tennessee's playoff odds from 70.9% to 44.5% if it loses to LSU.
Elsewhere in the SEC, No. 1 Georgia at No. 21 South Carolina and No. 16 Kentucky at Missouri are both intriguing. If the Bulldogs crush the Gamecocks, does that drop South Carolina out of the top 25? If so, it's a hit to the resumes of Alabama and Tennessee. The same would be true if Kentucky loses to Missouri on the road. Georgia can clinch a spot in the SEC Championship Game, too, if it avoids a letdown against a hungry South Carolina team coming off an embarrassing loss to Arkansas.
In the Big Ten, there are four games that stand out. Can Kyle Whittingham quiet the outside noise and secure a marquee win over No. 4 UCLA? If he does, it puts a lot of pressure on UCLA to win its regular-season finale against USC. No. 14 Ohio State at Nebraska and No. 15 Iowa at Illinois are opportunities for two playoff bubble teams to make their cases for why they deserve a spot. Sterling believes a win over Kevin Vallejos at UFC Fight Night in Qatar could put him in line for a second title shot in as many divisions
By

LAS VEGAS -- A UFC title run didn't earn Aljamain Sterling the respect it should've. Fans haven't warmly embraced him or his many accomplishments as one of the best bantamweights ever. But the "Funk Master" is stubborn and talented enough to try and achieve something that even his boldest cynics would have trouble disputing.
Sterling fights Kevin Vallejos in Saturday's UFC Fight Night co-main event in Qatar. A victory could put the former bantamweight champion in line to challenge Alexander Volkanovski for the featherweight title, giving Sterling a chance to join the exclusive club of UFC fighters who have won two weight class titles. It's an opportunity the No. 4-ranked featherweight contender never expected to have this late in his career.
Sterling has already accomplished more than enough to retire comfortably. He holds UFC bantamweight records for most consecutive wins and title defenses. Yet the chance to add another championship to his resume has kept him sharp. He knows better than most that winning a title doesn't always win over critics, but the numbers on his side are irrefutable.
"I think it's just the history books," Sterling told CBS Sports. "I have enough money where I'm more than comfortable. More money is always good, though. But I think it's just the history. That's really it. Just setting records, doing something that no one could ever take away from you."

Sterling has obsessed over accolades since his amateur wrestling days, when he never achieved the championship success he wanted. That disappointment fueled his MMA career, eventually carrying him to the UFC bantamweight title and three successful defenses. Moving up to featherweight allowed him to repeat that cycle all over again.
"I came up short in my amateur wrestling career; I never won a national title, never got to go to the state tournament, and it just always made me hungrier to keep pushing," Sterling said. "I became a UFC champ, and after setting the records, I came up short in my last one. Then I went up to 45, and now here's a new goal. I could become a two-division champion. I think that's a special feat in itself. People can talk and say whatever they want, but numbers don't lie. So for me, that's what it's all about."
Sterling's relationship with UFC fans has been complicated since he first won the bantamweight title in 2021. Petr Yan handed him the championship after striking him with  a blatantly illegal knee, resulting in a disqualification. Sterling was accused of exaggerating the damage to win a title in a fight he was clearly losing. The stink lingered even after the "Funk Master" defeated Yan in their rematch and successfully defended the championship against T.J. Dillashaw and Henry Cejudo.
His reign ended just as frustratingly. Sterling faced Sean O'Malley on a quick turnaround despite dealing with injuries, losing by second-round TKO. He then moved to featherweight without a red-carpet rollout for his 135-pound accomplishments. Sterling isn't deaf to the accusations that he isn't as good as his record suggests, despite repeatedly beating fighters whom his critics hold in high regard.
"People still want to find a way to chip away at what I've done. Dude, look at the numbers. Clearly, I'm better than what you think," Sterling said. "I can't be that bad if I'm beating all these other guys that you rate at this level. It is what it is. I'm comfortable in my own skin. I know I've done enough. And again, for me, numbers don't lie. So if you want to say this or that, I go, 'OK, but what does it say in the history books?' So go argue with the numbers, don't argue with me."
